preamble: Backing of the front rounded vowel [y] to [u] keeps rounding while retracting the tongue. Its clearest documented case is Middle English: in the southern West Midlands and the Southwest, Old English /y/ often became /u/, especially near labials and palato-alveolars, and these u-forms entered Standard English (shut, much, cudgel, church), where the vowel later developed to /ʌ/ or /ɜː/.

examples.note: Old English /y/ > Middle English /u/; modern /ʌ/ by the later FOOT–STRUT split.
The variant miċel shows the competing unrounding y > i.

sources: Wiktionary (2026). Category:English terms with /ʌ~ʊ/ for Old English /y/. https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Category:English_terms_with_/%CA%8C~%CA%8A/_for_Old_English_/y/
